query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A carefully controlled post-solidification aging heat treatment at an optimized temperature (400–600°C) and duration induces fine, evenly dispersed nano-precipitates at the eutectic interfaces, which can simultaneously increase the strength and ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys fabricated by standard casting methods that exhibit a lamellar or rod‐like microstructure with soft FCC and hard BCC/intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-solidification aging heat treatment with temperature in the 400–600°C range and an optimized duration to promote controlled nano-precipitation at the eutectic interfaces.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed on as-cast EHEAs under standard processing conditions; the aging temperatures should be maintained between 400–600°C with time durations varied to determine the process window that yields fine, dispersed precipitates without coarsening, with testing conducted at room temperature under quasi-static tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of uniformly distributed, nano-scale precipitates at the eutectic interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The nano-precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion, enhancing strength via precipitation strengthening; simultaneously, their fine scale and dispersion help maintain or even improve ductility by preventing premature localization of deformation and encouraging strain hardening across the dual-phase microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast (or standard annealed) alloy, the aged EHEA is predicted to exhibit an increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths while also showing maintained or improved ductility, though the exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain and will depend on the precise aging parameters and alloy composition.
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties of the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy before any specialized aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only when aging parameters are within the optimal window (approximately 400–600°C and an appropriate time to avoid coarsening). Aging outside this range (too high temperature or too long a time) may dissolve the nano-precipitates or cause coarsening, leading to loss of the simultaneous improvement in strength and ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in strength and ductility is uncertain and may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and exact aging conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples using standard casting methods. Subject subsets of the samples to post-solidification aging treatments at various temperatures (within and outside the 400–600°C window) and durations. Characterize the microstructures using TEM and EBSD to quantify the size and distribution of nano-precipitates at the eutectic interfaces. Perform quasi-static tensile testing and hardness measurements to compare the mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation) of the heat-treated samples with the as-cast baseline.
measurements: Nano-precipitate size and spatial distribution (TEM, EBSD)
Yield Strength and Ultimate Tensile Strength (tensile testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples aged within the optimized 400–600°C window do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength (yield and/or ultimate tensile strength) and ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if they exhibit a trade-off (e.g., increased strength but reduced ductility), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.

Presently, different kinds of topologically close-packed (TCP) phases, such as σ, μ, Laves, etc. are observed in HEAs [,]. Adding this reinforcing phase to the FCC high entropy alloys can significantly increase their strength, but at the same time significantly reduce their plasticity []. Based on the precipitation strengthening effect, the most important thing is to control the morphology and distribution of the precipitated phase, and then to alleviate their harmful effects on ductility. As reported, the size and distribution of the reinforcing phase is very sensitive to heat treatment conditions. Gwalani et al. [] reported that the L12 Ni3 (Ti, Al) nano-precipitates in the Al0.3CrFeCoNi alloy can only be stably present in the temperature range of 500–600 °C. As the temperatures above ~700 °C, these precipitates are dissolved and replaced by coarser ordered B2 precipitates. Liu et al. [] reported that the precipitated nano σ phase formed during the heat treatment at 850–900 °C can simultaneously increase the strength and plasticity of the CoCrFeNiMo0.3 alloy. Ming et al. [] reported that the Cr15Fe20Co35Ni20Mo10 HEA exhibit a superb strength–ductility combination by precipitation

chosen.technique: systematic heat treatment experiments with subsequent TEM/EBSD microstructural analysis and mechanical testing (tensile and hardness measurements)
chosen.conditions: using eutectic high-entropy alloys prepared by standard casting methods and then aged at 400–600°C for optimized durations, comparing results to the as-cast (or standard annealed) baseline
chosen.why: This intervention directly targets the microstructural balance that underpins the simultaneous improvement of strength and ductility by inducing a controlled nano-precipitation mechanism. The approach fills the niche by inverting previous studies that may have optimized only one property or relied on simplified processing, and employs well-established experimental techniques in materials science to generate clear, falsifiable outcomes.
